bio.life: Vera Turán Sós was born in Budapest on 11 September 1930 into the golden age of Hungarian mathematics, taught at Eötvös Loránd University and the Alfréd Rényi Institute for the length of a long century of a career, and stood at the center of the Budapest school: a decades-long collaborator of Erdős (more than thirty joint papers), and wife of Pál Turán, the analytic number theorist — mathematics ran through every room of the house. She was elected to the Hungarian Academy and honored across Europe; she died in Budapest on 22 January 2023, at ninety-two.
bio.mathematics: As a doctoral-age mathematician in 1957–58 she proved Steinhaus's three-distance conjecture: the points α, 2α, …, Nα on the circle cut it into arcs of at most three lengths, the longest the sum of the other two — with the whole pattern governed by the continued-fraction convergents of α. It is the theorem this site's three-distance displays run, φ's arcs being the most evenly balanced possible, and she shares the credit line honestly with Świerczkowski and Surányi, who proved it independently at nearly the same moment. In extremal graph theory the Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem bounds how dense a graph can be without containing a complete bipartite pattern — a cornerstone cited daily; with Erdős she shaped Ramsey–Turán theory; with Chung and Graham she characterized quasi-random graphs, the discovery that many definitions of 'random-like' coincide — a founding stone of modern combinatorics' pseudorandomness industry.
bio.legacy: Three-distance, Kővári–Sós–Turán, quasi-randomness: three permanent walls in three different rooms. The Athenaeum records her as the great continuer — the mathematician through whom the Budapest tradition of Erdős and Turán flowed into the twenty-first century.

bio.life: Harry Kesten was born Harry Kesten in Duisburg, Germany, on 19 November 1931; his Jewish family fled to the Netherlands in 1933, and he survived the war and occupation there as a child. He came to Cornell for his doctorate under Mark Kac — his 1958 thesis on random walks on groups introduced what is now Kesten's criterion for amenability — and after a brief period elsewhere returned to Cornell for good. Universally regarded as the deepest probabilist of his generation on discrete structures, and personally famous for modesty and generosity, he died in Ithaca on 29 March 2019.
bio.mathematics: Kesten's 1980 theorem is one of probability's monuments: the critical probability for bond percolation on the square lattice is exactly 1/2. Simulation and duality heuristics had pointed at the value for twenty years; Kesten proved it, and his methods — with the follow-up that at criticality no infinite cluster exists in two dimensions — created rigorous percolation theory as this site's percolation lab presents it: the measured crossing threshold 0.499… standing beside the proven 1/2, register-labeled. His thesis gave amenability a spectral characterization; the Kesten–Stigum theorem settled when branching processes grow cleanly; first-passage percolation, random walks in random environments, Diophantine approximation (the Erdős–Kesten circle), and the DLA growth bounds all carry central results of his. He won the Abel-adjacent honors of his field (Pólya Prize, Steele Prize) and trained a school.
bio.legacy: The exact 1/2 is this site's showcase of proof beating simulation at its own game — the simulations were right, and only the theorem made it knowledge. Kesten is the Athenaeum's model of the probabilist as prover: no heuristic left standing unproved or unrefuted.

bio.life: Stanisław Świerczkowski was born in Toruń, Poland, on 16 July 1932, into a life that the twentieth century kept relocating: educated in Wrocław in the postwar Polish school around Steinhaus's circle, he held posts in Glasgow, Dundee, the United States, Australia (ANU), and finally, for many years, Sultan Qaboos University in Oman — a mathematical career conducted on four continents. He died in 2015. His autobiography, 'Looking Astern,' records the journey with the same clarity he wrote proofs in.
bio.mathematics: In 1958, at twenty-six, he proved Steinhaus's three-distance conjecture — independently of Vera Sós and at essentially the same time, by a different route: the points α, 2α, …, Nα partition the circle into arcs of at most three distinct lengths. The theorem carries both their names in the literature, and this site's displays credit both. His range then went where his travels did: the Świerczkowski non-tetratorus theorem (a chain of regular tetrahedra can never close into a loop — a small, perfect impossibility result), work on abstract algebra and measurable functions, and, remarkably, a late-career second act in logic: his 2003 monograph proved Gödel's incompleteness theorems from hereditarily finite sets with such care and completeness that it became the direct blueprint for Lawrence Paulson's machine formalization of the incompleteness theorems in Isabelle — one of formal verification's landmark achievements.
bio.legacy: A theorem shared with Sós that this site draws live, and a proof of Gödel written so honestly that a computer could check it: Świerczkowski connects the Athenaeum's two deepest themes — visible structure and machine-verified truth — in one itinerant career.

legends.claim: His Gödel monograph was the blueprint for the Isabelle formalization
legends.note: Paulson's 2014 formalization papers state explicitly that they follow Świerczkowski's 2003 development.

bio.life: Norman Laurence Gilbreath was born in 1936 and has conducted one of the stranger double careers in this hall: research mathematician (UCLA-trained, longtime RAND affiliation) and world-class close-up magician. As a living person he receives the Athenaeum's emblem treatment, and this profile keeps to the public record — which in his case is genuinely two records, one in number theory and one in conjuring.
bio.mathematics: In 1958, doodling on a napkin — his own account — Gilbreath computed the absolute differences of consecutive primes, then the differences of those, and so on, and noticed that every row after the first seems to begin with 1. That observation, the Gilbreath conjecture (Proth had claimed it in 1878 with a faulty proof), has been verified to enormous depth — Odlyzko checked the first 3.4 × 10^11 rows in 1993 — and remains unproved: OPEN, exactly as this site's Gilbreath lab labels it while letting visitors race the triangle themselves. In magic, the Gilbreath principle — riffle-shuffle a deck prepared in alternating pattern and the pattern survives in a precise combinatorial sense — is among the most celebrated mathematical principles in card conjuring, studied in Martin Gardner's columns and in the Diaconis–Graham book on mathematical magic; its second-order generalization is genuinely deep combinatorics on sequences.
bio.legacy: Two immortalities from pattern-noticing: an open problem on the primes' differences and a shuffle principle magicians will perform as long as cards exist. The Athenaeum shelves him as its witness that noticing — on a napkin, at a card table — is a mathematical act.

legends.claim: The napkin origin of the conjecture
legends.note: Gilbreath's own account of the 1958 observation; charming, self-reported, and so labeled.
François Proth published the assertion with an incorrect proof; the conjecture properly bears Gilbreath's name from the 1958 revival.

works.title: The Gilbreath conjecture (circulated 1958)

bio.life: Abraham Ziv shares with his 1961 co-author Ginzburg the strange fate of a name permanently attached to a first-course theorem while the person behind it remains nearly invisible to the literature. The documented record: an Israeli mathematician, co-author of the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv theorem in 1961, who spent his later career at IBM's Haifa Research Laboratory working on the accuracy of floating-point computation. He is a different person from Jacob Ziv of Lempel–Ziv compression fame — a disambiguation the Athenaeum makes explicitly, since the confusion is common. Out of caution with the thin record, no dates are asserted and the emblem treatment is used.
bio.mathematics: Two contributions, remarkably far apart. The 1961 EGZ theorem — any 2n − 1 integers contain n whose sum is divisible by n, the bound exact — founded zero-sum combinatorics and is machine-verified in this site's corpus. Three decades later, 'Ziv's strategy' (1991) solved a practical impossibility elegantly: correctly rounding transcendental functions seems to require unbounded precision (the 'table-maker's dilemma'), but Ziv showed that recomputing at successively higher precision until the rounding is provably unambiguous terminates fast in practice — the onion-peeling algorithm inside IBM's and many subsequent correctly-rounded mathematical libraries. Every provably-correctly-rounded elementary function in modern computing owes the technique a citation.
bio.legacy: A zero-sum cornerstone in pure combinatorics and the standard trick behind correctly-rounded libraries: Ziv's two legacies bracket this site's own span — verified theorems on one side, trustworthy computation on the other.

legends.note: Different people; the compression pioneer is Jacob Ziv (1931–2023). The EGZ/floating-point Ziv is Abraham.

works.title: Theorem in the additive number theory (with P. Erdős and A. Ginzburg)

works.note: ACM TOMS: Ziv's rounding strategy, the engine of correctly-rounded libm implementations.

bio.life: Hugh Lowell Montgomery was born in Muncie, Indiana, on 26 August 1944, studied at Illinois and then Cambridge — where his doctoral work grew under Harold Davenport in the last years of Davenport's life — and has spent his career at the University of Michigan, training a substantial share of America's analytic number theorists. As a living person he receives the Athenaeum's emblem treatment and a public-record profile.
bio.mathematics: In 1972, assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, Montgomery computed how the normalized spacings between zeta zeros are correlated and conjectured the pair-correlation function 1 − (sin πu / πu)²: the zeros repel each other. Over tea at the Institute for Advanced Study, Freeman Dyson recognized the function instantly as the pair correlation of eigenvalues in the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble — the exchange, documented by both participants, that fused random-matrix theory with the zeta function and created the spectral program this site's pair-correlation lab and Observatory chapters walk. The conjecture stands unproved (OPEN in this site's ledgers) but is verified numerically to extraordinary precision by Odlyzko's computations. Montgomery's wider work is foundational infrastructure: the large sieve brought to sharpness with Vaughan, the Montgomery–Vaughan inequality, zero-density estimates, and the graduate text (Multiplicative Number Theory I, with Vaughan) that teaches the field.
bio.legacy: The pair-correlation conjecture is the strongest bridge yet built between the primes and quantum spectra — the reason 'the zeros hum like a random matrix' is a sentence this site can display with evidence. Montgomery built the bridge's arithmetic side.

legends.note: Recounted consistently by both men in interviews and print; the founding anecdote of arithmetic quantum chaos.

bio.life: Andrew Michael Odlyzko was born in Tarnów, Poland, on 23 July 1949, emigrated to the United States, and spent twenty-six years at Bell Labs — the golden-age industrial laboratory where his job description was, in effect, curiosity — before moving to the University of Minnesota, where he has also written influentially on network economics, the history of financial bubbles, and why 'content is not king.' As a living person he receives the emblem treatment and a public-record profile.
bio.mathematics: Odlyzko is the great empiricist of the zeta function. His computations of zeros at heights around the 10^20th and 10^22nd zero — batches of tens of millions, computed to high precision with algorithms he co-designed (the Odlyzko–Schönhage method makes bulk zero computation feasible) — turned the Montgomery–Dyson pair-correlation conjecture from a plausible identity into one of the most precisely tested unproved statements in mathematics: the zeros' spacing statistics match GUE predictions to the resolution of the plots. This site's Observatory and dataset pipeline live directly downstream. In 1985, with Herman te Riele, he disproved the Mertens conjecture — no counterexample exhibited, only proof that one exists — mathematics' cleanest demonstration that 10^10 confirmations can precede falsity. He also verified Gilbreath's conjecture to depth 3.4 × 10^11 and did foundational work in cryptography (discrete logarithms) and combinatorics.
bio.legacy: The site's twin mottos — 'compute honestly' and 'the data is not the theorem' — have no better patron: Odlyzko both produced the era's best numerical evidence and personally disproved a conjecture the evidence favored. Empiricism with a conscience.

bio.life: Thomas Callister Hales was born on 4 June 1958 in San Antonio, Texas, studied at Stanford, Cambridge, and Princeton, and has held chairs at Michigan and Pittsburgh. As a living person he receives the Athenaeum's emblem treatment; his public record happens to contain one of the pivotal stories in the history of mathematical certainty, which this profile tells.
bio.mathematics: In 1998 Hales (with his student Samuel Ferguson) announced a proof of the Kepler conjecture: no packing of equal spheres beats face-centered cubic's π/√18. The proof mixed human geometry with thousands of linear programs. The Annals' referee panel, after four years, reported it was '99% certain' the proof was correct — and could not certify the rest. Hales' response created a field: the Flyspeck project, a decade-long formalization of the entire proof in the HOL Light and Isabelle proof assistants, completed 14 August 2014 — after which there was nothing left to doubt but the proof checkers' half-page kernels. He had already formally verified the Jordan curve theorem along the way, proved the honeycomb conjecture (1999) — hexagons are the cheapest way to partition the plane into unit areas — and later launched the Formal Abstracts project to make mathematical statements machine-readable at scale. The 400-year arc from Kepler's 1611 snowflake essay to Flyspeck's 2014 QED is the founding parable of formal verification.
bio.legacy: This site's entire PROVED register — machine-checked, referee-independent — operates in the world Flyspeck demonstrated was possible. The sphere-packing lab tells Kepler's conjecture as a story that ends in Hales' formal proof; the Athenaeum records him as the mathematician who, told '99% certain,' decided that was not a number mathematics should accept.

legends.note: Described in the Annals editorial process and by panel chair Gábor Fejes Tóth; the phrase is part of the published record of the episode.

bio.life: Hao Huang is a contemporary combinatorialist — doctorate at UCLA under Benny Sudakov, positions at Emory University and then the National University of Singapore. As a living person he receives the emblem treatment, and the Athenaeum confines itself to the public mathematical record, which in his case centers on one of the most celebrated short proofs of the century.
bio.mathematics: The sensitivity conjecture — that for Boolean functions, sensitivity is polynomially related to the other complexity measures (block sensitivity, degree) — stood open for thirty years as the stubborn gap in the otherwise-unified theory of Boolean complexity. In July 2019 Huang closed it in under two pages. The proof is pure spectral graph theory of the kind this site's hypercube lab animates: sign the hypercube's adjacency matrix so that its square is n·I (the signing is a Clifford-algebra trick), conclude the eigenvalues are ±√n, and apply Cauchy's eigenvalue interlacing to force any induced subgraph on more than half the vertices to contain a vertex of degree at least √n — which, by a 1992 reduction of Gotsman and Linial, is exactly the sensitivity conjecture. Mathematicians' near-universal reaction — 'it fits in a tweet' — was literal: the proof circulated complete on social media within days.
bio.legacy: The Athenaeum's freshest exhibit that a decades-open problem can fall to two beautiful pages. The signed-hypercube spectrum is precisely the computation this site's sensitivity lab performs live, interlacing and all — a frontier theorem young enough that its author's career is still being written.

works.title: Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture

bio.life: Maryna Viazovska was born in Kyiv, Ukraine, on 2 December 1984, trained in Kyiv's mathematical olympiad tradition and then at Kaiserslautern and Bonn, and holds the chair of number theory at EPFL in Lausanne. In 2022 she received the Fields Medal — the second woman in the medal's history — months after her home city was attacked in the Russian invasion of Ukraine. As a living person she receives the emblem treatment, and this profile keeps to the public record.
bio.mathematics: In March 2016 Viazovska solved the sphere-packing problem in dimension eight: the E₈ lattice is optimal. Where dimension three (Kepler–Hales) had required hundreds of pages and thousands of computer programs, her proof is twenty-three pages of classical beauty: she constructed the 'magic function' — built from modular forms — whose existence Cohn and Elkies had shown in 2003 would make their linear-programming bound exactly tight at E₈. The function's construction was the missing art. Within a week she and collaborators (Cohn, Kumar, Miller, Radchenko) adapted it to dimension twenty-four for the Leech lattice. No other dimension above three is solved; the same magic-function method has since produced universal optimality results for E₈ and Leech (ground states among all point configurations, not just packings) and new interpolation theorems in Fourier analysis.
bio.legacy: This site's sphere-packing story ends its 400-year arc — Kepler's greengrocer, Hales' computers — with Viazovska's proof that in dimensions 8 and 24 the answer is a short poem: the exceptional lattices win, provably, by modular magic. The Athenaeum's youngest permanent wall.

bio.life: Helmut Vogel is known to this site — and to everyone who has ever plotted a sunflower — for a single 1979 paper in Mathematical Biosciences. The biographical record in the mathematical literature is thin; the standard identification is with the German physicist of that name associated with the Technical University of Munich, but the Athenaeum declines to assert dates it cannot source. Out of caution he receives the emblem treatment and a strictly public-record profile.
bio.mathematics: Vogel's paper, 'A better way to construct the sunflower head,' distilled phyllotaxis into two lines: place floret n at angle n × 137.508° (the golden angle) and radius c√n. The square root keeps the area allotted to each floret constant — new growth pushes old growth outward exactly enough — and the golden angle, being the 'most irrational' rotation by Hurwitz's theorem, prevents the florets from ever aligning into wasteful radial spokes. The visible result: spiral families whose counts are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, matching real sunflower heads. The model is descriptive, not mechanistic — the developmental dynamics were supplied later by Douady and Couder's experiments and models in the 1990s — but as a generative recipe it is definitive, and it is precisely the formula this site's phyllotaxis lab runs live, golden angle adjustable, Fibonacci spirals emerging and collapsing as the visitor detunes φ.
bio.legacy: One formula that every mathematical-art generator, botany textbook, and procedural-graphics library now contains: Vogel's spiral is how humanity draws the sunflower. The Athenaeum honors the well-made small thing.
